newsitem.title: UK: Halifax windfall won't bloat UK economy.
newsitem.headline: Halifax windfall won't bloat UK economy.

text.p: This year's wave of British building society flotations could pump close to 30 billion pounds ($49.1 billion) into the economy, but the government, central bank and independent analysts are relaxed about the economic impact of the windfall cash.

Halifax Plc on Monday paid out an average 2,294 pounds to its 7.6 million savers and borrowers, a total of around 17 billion pounds which far exceeds the estimate made earlier in the year of a 12 billion pound windfall. There are fears in some quarters however the bonus cash could trigger a massive consumer-led spending spree.
The Alliance & Leicester in April also far exceeded estimates when savers and lenders received 3.0 billion pounds instead of the 2.5 billion pounds forecast.

The government and the Bank of England have indicated that while they are monitoring the situation, they see no need for alarm. But some economists said on Monday the authorities might be guilty of underestimating the impact of the windfalls.
"It looks like the Bank, Treasury along with the City is erring on the aide of caution," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.

"Earlier this year it was taken that the flotations would total 20 billion pounds. Now looks like 28 billion pounds is Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said fast growth in consumer spending was a risk to inflation when he agreed to raise interest rates by a quarter point to 6.25 percent in early May, but he made no direct mention of windfall payments.

Analysts said the government appears to have adopted the economically orthodox view of the previous government. It assumed most of the money will be saved, not spent, and the effect on consumer spending and GDP would be relatively small.
The Bank of England said in the May inflation report it assumed only between five and 10 percent of the payments would be spent this year, although it acknowledged the risk was on the upside.
The Bank, along with many other economists, has had to look again at forecasts of the total in windfall payments likely to made during the year after the A&L float surpassed expectations.
"Since the publication of the February Report, the expected payouts in 1997 have increased from 21 billion pounds to 28 billion pounds," it said in the May report.

The next big flotation is due next week time when the Norwich Union Building Society floats. It is now likely to pay out much more than the 1.5 billion pounds estimated by economists earlier this year.
But despite the higher-than-expected payouts, many economists still believe the impact on overall spending and inflation will be minimal.
They agree with the mainstream economic theory which suggests people view windfalls as one-off boosts to income and spend them gradually over many years.
A survey carried out by pollster Mori in February commissioned by U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers, which surveyed 3,685 people expecting to receive windfall payments this year, bares this out.
It found that between 10 and 25 percent of windfalls will be spent in the year, and Salomon concluded that the outcome will be in the lower part of the range.

However, the survey was carried out before the first flotation and underestimated the number of early share sellers. It said only 12 percent said they would sell shares straight away compared with the 27 percent who immediately sold A&L shares in April.
Economists are aware of the risk involved in forecasting the impact.

"This is uncharted territory and the first time such a huge transfer of wealth has been made into the personal sector, so we are saying up to 25 percent could be spent," said Stephen Radley, chief economist at the Henley Centre for Forecasting.
But even with this generous forecast, he said the inflationary risk is small with durable goods and foreign travel set to become the chief beneficiaries.
Inflation in goods is running at a very low rate, up by just 1.7 percent in the year to April, with durable goods showing even lower price rises.
"Although the consumer sector is very buoyant, retailers are still finding it very hard to raise the price of goods. Consumers are still very resistant to higher prices," said Radley.
